content.title: About
content.content: Chia seeds are edible seeds of the plant Salvia hispanica, native to Mexico and Guatemala. They are tiny (about 2 mm), oval‑shaped, and dark brown to black. Chia is nutrient‑dense, forms a gel when mixed with liquid, and is widely used in health‑focused diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chia was a staple food for the ancient Aztec and Maya civilizations, valued for its energy‑boosting properties.
The seeds can absorb up to 12 times their weight in water, creating a gelatinous texture popular in smoothies and puddings.
Chia is not a nut, making it suitable for people with nut allergies.
In the 1990s, chia gained popularity as a “superfood” across Europe and the United States.
Chia is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids in the form of alpha‑linolenic acid (ALA).

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Chia provides alpha‑linolenic acid, which supports heart and vascular health.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: About 20 % of the seed’s weight is protein, beneficial for muscle and tissue maintenance.

items.title: Loaded with antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds and quercetin protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Chia contains calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, essential for strong bones.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to chia seeds.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: High fiber intake can cause bloating, gas, or diarrhea if not accompanied by adequate fluid consumption.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Because of its omega‑3 content, chia may enhance the effects of anticoagulant drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add chia seeds to smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal, or baked goods, or make a pudding by soaking them in milk or water for 10‑15 minutes. They also work as a thickener for sauces and dressings. Sprinkle them on salads or use in energy bars.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store chia seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.
